#4822. Walking, Yoga, or Zumba? Which Exercises Help Relieve Menopause Mood Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Physical activity may help support mood and improve quality of life during the menopause transition, according to a study published on October 13 in Menopause, the journal of the Menopause Society.

This review of 12 clinical trials involving over 1,000 people ages 40 to 65 found that both aerobic and mind-body exercises may be associated with reduced depressive symptoms and improved well-being.

It is common for individuals to experience psychological symptoms during menopause, including depression, anxiety, low mood, stress, and difficulty with thinking and memory. These symptoms can have a significant effect on quality of life, with an estimated 1 in 10 women leaving work due to menopause symptoms.

This study found that regular physical activity may help improve certain psychological symptoms and overall quality of life during menopause.

The types of physical activity in the review were broken into two categories: aerobic-based exercise (ABIs) and mind-body activities (MBAs).

The researchers found that ABIs showed the strongest effects on reducing depressive symptoms and improving overall quality of life. This may be particularly relevant during perimenopause when women may be more vulnerable to mood instability due to estrogen fluctuations.

Sherry Ross, MD, board certified OB/GYN and Women’s Health Expert at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, pointed out that there are various ways that ABIs can have positive effects.

Ross explained that aerobic exercise may help improve menopausal symptoms through several mechanisms, including the release of endorphins, reduced inflammation, improved cholesterol levels, and better regulation of body temperature and sleep cycles.

MBAs were shown to have a greater effect on improving psychological quality of life. These exercises involve mindfulness, body awareness, and breathwork. They may help improve emotional regulation.

ABIs tended to require fewer sessions. This may mean these types of exercises are easier to fit in, especially if you are facing time or energy constraints. For example, in one trial, participants were instructed to walk for 30 minutes, three times per week. In another trial, participants attended three hour-long Zumba classes per week.

In contrast, one trial using MBAs instructed participants to attend two 75-minute yoga classes each week, and another had participants attend daily one-hour yoga classes.

Stephanie Faubion, MD, Director for the Mayo Clinic Center for Women’s Health and Medical Director for The Menopause Society, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline that these findings are encouraging.

However, she also cautioned that this was a relatively small body of evidence. “While physical activity is an important component of a healthy lifestyle during midlife, I would be cautious about interpreting these findings to mean that exercise is a treatment for depression related specifically to menopause,” she said.

Research has shown that physical activity can positively affect mental health. Studies have also found that regular exercise can help improve symptoms of depression and anxiety.

Faubion told Healthline that, broadly speaking, regular physical activity may support mood through multiple pathways, including better sleep, improved physical function, and overall well-being.

However, she also noted that this study cannot tell us precisely why the improvements occurred or whether aerobic exercise is superior to other forms of activity.

Faubion said that recommending physical activity during and after menopause extends well beyond mood.

“Physical activity is important for cardiovascular and metabolic health, maintaining muscle mass and physical function, and supporting bone health,” she said.

“These become particularly important at midlife as women experience age- and menopause-related changes in body composition, bone, and cardiometabolic health,” Faubion added.

Ross agreed that physical activity is important for more than just mood and mental health improvement. She also noted that there are other types of exercise beyond ABIs and MBAs that can benefit people during menopause:

“These types of activities help with weight loss or allow women to maintain a healthy weight. If you are not ready for aerobic exercises, stretching and simple exercises help with balance and stability,” Ross said.

Faubion told Healthline that physical activity is an important part of healthy aging and should be encouraged during the menopause transition, but it should not be suggested that women can simply exercise their way out of significant depression or other bothersome menopause symptoms.

“Women experiencing persistent depression, anxiety, or symptoms that interfere with their quality of life should seek evaluation and discuss the full range of evidence-based treatment options with their healthcare clinician,” Faubion said.

#4821. Measurability Bias, HR Tech, and Work: The Unholy Trinity

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Michelle Quirk

In its very design, industrial/organizational (I/O) psychology (a.k.a. "psychology of work") reveals something nuanced and supremely relevant about what drives behavior in organizations.

Industrial psychology treats the individual as the unit of measure, while organizational psychology measures the group. The former tends to be measured quantitatively, while the latter tends to be measured qualitatively.

So, what falls on the “I” side (selection, training, performance management, core human resources [HR]) is very different than what falls on the “O” side (leadership, motivation, organizational development, culture).

From a technological investment point of view, “I” has a lot going for it. For starters, only quantitative data flows cleanly into a system of record, so there’s a built-in motivation for organizational use. But that’s not even the half of it.

Measurability bias describes the tendency of people to prioritize easily quantifiable metrics over qualitative factors that are difficult, if not impossible, to measure.

It’s not hard to understand why. Easily quantifiable metrics require a lot less thinking and ostensibly provide a lot more certainty. (Of course, “ostensibly” is necessary because they’re so often applied incorrectly.)

Human beings hate uncertainty at a cellular level, and we often embrace whatever we can to reassure ourselves that we are making the right decision. This tendency is heightened in professional settings because the stakes are so high. We go out of our way to leverage quantitative data for guidance, cover, and reassurance.

That’s why “I” gets the prize, and it’s not hard to see why. According to analysis by 451 Research, less than 2 percent of sales of the $94 billion HR technology market goes to the qualitatively measured “O” constructs.

The same is true for investment. HRO Today tracked investment in 2025 and found that nearly all of the $3.75 billion went into the “I” side.

And where the technology and investment go, so goes the human attention.

As a result, constructs like leadership, motivation, and organizational culture receive comparably tiny resources and attention. Even something squarely on the “O” side like employee engagement, which had a brief run as the HR metric du jour, only did so because it offered a quantitative measure of a qualitative construct.

If the bias for easily quantifiable metrics creates a disincentive to pursue qualitative constructs through technology and investment, can we at least assume that the upside is that we’re making great decisions, grounded in data and analytics? Nope.

What does the peer-reviewed research say about the efficacy of HR technology and investment on the “I” side of I/O psychology? There’s not a lot of it. What we do know isn’t promising.

Hiring? Research from Bauer and SHRM (2010) indicates that half of senior hires fail within 18 months, and that 50 percent of hourly workers leave within the first 120 days.

Training? A study by Saks and Belcourt (2006) found that two out of three trainees were not using the training one year later.

One could argue that HR technology has adopted these same practices and merely reproduced them at greater scale, as Capelli did in his HBR article (2019).

Performance management? Scullen, Mount, and Goff (2000) found that between 53 and 62 percent of variance in feedback is reflective of the feedback provider, not the feedback recipient. In other words, the feedback tells us more about the person providing it than the person receiving it. Kluger and DeNisi (1996) found that feedback actually harms performance more than a third of the time.

That research may be dated, but it reveals something fundamental about human behavior that performance management still fails to take into account.

There’s an ironic twist, to boot. What gets in the way of the efficacy of the heavily weighted technological investment in industrial psychology driven by measurement bias? Measurement bias.

What gets measured in selection? Volume of applications and time to fill. What doesn’t get measured? Outcomes. For training, it’s completion and satisfaction. And most performance management efforts have little to do with performance.

We don’t measure the outcomes of hiring decisions because it’s too hard to do and takes way too long. The same is true for training outcomes. By the time we know, we think (incorrectly) it’s too late to do anything about it. And performance management? The logical overriding motivation for managers is not to hurt anyone’s motivation moving forward, and that's not what performance management is designed to do.

Concerns about the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) on people and work are as well-founded as they are widespread. But they also overlook how AI can help us to be more human.

The ability to analyze qualitative data sets at a breakneck speed means that practitioners finally have access to the types of evidence that provide demonstrable proof of impact and return on investment (ROI).

Proper use of AI can tell us more about leadership, motivation, and culture at an organization than we have ever known. And it can do so in ways that support great decision-making, both strategically and tactically.

Our company is designing HR tools that can provide the benefits of psychological safety (surfacing truth) where it does not exist. We achieve this by summarizing anonymous qualitative data in real time, carefully framing the summary to avoid finger-pointing and surfacing the most productive steps forward.

We accelerate team decision-making by summarizing everyone’s opinion before the conversation begins, using pre-surfaced conflicting points of view as the starting point for discussions. We use AI to nudge people into creating better and more aligned goals across the organization. And now we can surface the way work really gets done through a combination of AI-document reviews and AI-assisted human-led interviews.

These are but a few examples of how AI can revolutionize HR and HR tech: by creating better sources of qualitative data. It may sound abstract, but the positive effect on work will be profound.

Yes, the impact that AI can have on the future of work is very scary. But interestingly, it also just might make the future of work way more human.

#4819. Do You Need a Vitamin B12 Supplement If You’re Taking a GLP-1?

Here’s why you don’t want vitamin B12 levels getting too low.

WHILE GLP-1 MEDS have been game changers for weight management, they’ve also introduced some challenges for people looking to lose weight. They reduce appetite and help you feel satisfied sooner, but that can make it more challenging to get all the nutrients your body needs.

One of the nutrients GLP-1 users may get less of is Vitamin B12. On social media, people discussing life on GLP-1s often bring up eating more foods high in B12 or recommending B12 supplements when complaints of side effects like fatigue and headaches come up.

Here’s what you need to know about vitamin B12 and GLP-1s along with how to make sure you’re getting enough.

VITAMIN B12, ALSO known as cobalamin, is an essential vitamin that cannot be produced by the body. It must come from food or supplements, says internist Jennifer Chung, MD.

Vitamin B12 supports several important bodily functions. It’s involved in the production of red blood cells, creation of DNA, and maintenance of a healthy nervous system. The demand for vitamin B12—the recommended daily intake of vitamin B12 for most adults is 2.4 micrograms—doesn’t go away even when you’re consuming fewer calories.

WHEN VITAMIN B12 levels drop too low, the effects can range from fatigue and weakness to more serious symptoms. Dr. Chung says this might involve anemia, which is a lack of healthy red blood cells to carry oxygen throughout the body, tingling or numbness in the hands and feet, and problems with balance or memory. If vitamin B12 deficiency persists, you may run the risk of permanent nerve damage.

TAKING A GLP-1 doesn’t automatically mean you’ll develop a B12 deficiency. It’s more of an indirect effect.

“GLP-1 medications are not known to reduce absorption of vitamin B12, unlike metformin, which interferes with the binding of vitamin B12 in the gastrointestinal tract,” explains Dr. Chung. “Instead, nutrient deficiencies with GLP-1 medications arise from a combination of eating less food, eating less dietary variety, delayed gastric emptying, and rapid weight loss.”

The common side effects people experience while taking a GLP-1—nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation—may also contribute to not getting enough vitamins like B12.

DOCTORS SAY A vitamin B12 supplement is worth considering for GLP-1 users, but it’s not a requirement.

“Several medical societies recommend that GLP-1 users consider supplementation with vitamin D, calcium, B12, and a multivitamin to reduce micronutrient deficiencies, but there is no universal recommendation,” says Dr. Chung.

Todd Worley, MD, bariatric surgeon and obesity medicine specialist at Houston Methodist Willowbrook Hospital, says the primary goal is to get enough of this essential nutrient through food.

B12 is found in a variety of animal-based foods, including beef, poultry, salmon, tuna, trout, eggs, clams, and dairy products. You can also find a comprehensive list of B12-rich foods here.

If a reduced appetite is making you unable to stomach enough food, then it’s time to consider a supplement. Another reason to consider a supplement is if you follow a plant-based or vegan diet.

Jacqueline Vernarelli, PhD, nutrition scientist at Sacred Heart University, says that unfortified plant foods aren’t a reliable source of the nutrient since vitamin B12 is primarily in animal-based foods. As a result, she recommends regularly incorporating B12-fortified foods, such as certain breakfast cereals and plant-based milks, to help meet your daily intake.

AGE AND SOME gastrointestinal conditions can also make it harder for your body to absorb the vitamin. “Conditions that reduce stomach acid increase with age, and stomach acid is needed to release vitamin B12 from protein in food so it can be absorbed,” says Dr. Chung. Guys might start feeling the effects of vitamin B12 deficiency in their 50s.

A B12 DEFICIENCY can be difficult to recognize because symptoms often develop gradually and may overlap with other issues. For example, you may attribute fatigue to not eating enough overall when it’s actually because you’re low on B12.

Dr. Chung recommends talking with the physician who prescribed your GLP-1 about any changes you’re feeling. They may recommend blood tests to check your B12 levels.

If blood tests confirm a B12 deficiency, your doctor may recommend dietary changes or a supplement.

Oral B12 supplements in capsule, tablet, or liquid form are often the first line of defense, with a common daily dose of 1,000 micrograms, says Dr. Chung. The reason supplements have larger doses than the recommended daily intake is because the body only absorbs a portion of the vitamin. Intramuscular B12 injections are also an option, but Dr. Worley says those are usually reserved for folks with absorption problems or more significant B12 deficiencies.

The right dose and form of B12 supplementation will depend on your individual needs. There’s no one-size-fits-all approach. Above all, Dr. Chung recommends being proactive and planning meals with enough B12 sources and keeping tabs on any signs of potential deficiencies. Losing weight shouldn’t mean sacrificing good health.

#4818. Why Do We Love Some Accents and Hate Others?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

We all have personal opinions about certain accents. Some make us swoon, while others make us cringe. They seem to inspire remarkably strong reactions for something as ordinary as the way a person pronounces their words.

To many people’s ears, a French accent might sound sophisticated and seductive, while a German accent is sometimes described as harsh or angry. A British accent may suggest refinement and education, but depending on where in Britain it comes from, it could also attract assumptions about someone’s intelligence or social class.

However, our reactions to accents often reveal more about our own prejudices than the people speaking. And these judgments aren't harmless: Accent bias can affect how people are perceived and treated.

An accent is the way we pronounce words that is influenced by our regional and social backgrounds. Everyone has one, although some people mistakenly believe they speak without an accent and that it’s everyone else who has one.

Accents carry powerful social associations and biases. (Stollznow, 2026) Perhaps the best-known example in British English is Received Pronunciation (RP), better known as the Queen’s English (now the King’s English) or BBC English. Popularized through the BBC’s newsreaders and presenters in the 1920s, this accent became associated with education, wealth, authority, and social privilege. To many people, it still sounds like the voice of someone who knows what they’re talking about.

But not all accents enjoy this same prestige. The Southern U.S. accent is sometimes unfairly associated with a lack of education, intelligence, or sophistication, reflecting longstanding stereotypes about the American South. Yet such perceptions depend on the context. In some communities, a Southern drawl might signal warmth, friendliness, authenticity, and regional pride. The same accent that one listener dismisses as unsophisticated might be valued by another as a marker of identity and belonging. Linguists call this covert prestige. This is the social value attached to ways of speaking that might not be considered prestigious by wider society, but are highly prized within particular communities.

Accent prejudice can also reflect much deeper social inequalities. African American English, for example, has long been stigmatized through racist stereotypes associating its speakers with laziness, poor education, and criminality. (Barrett, et al., 2022) These judgments have little to do with the dialect itself and everything to do with the prejudices faced by this group of people. Within this community, however, African American English is an important marker of identity, solidarity, and cultural pride. Its influence on jazz, R&B, hip hop, and popular culture also demonstrates its considerable cultural prestige beyond the community.

Our reactions to accents aren’t always about social class or race. Sometimes, we simply decide subjectively that certain languages sound more beautiful while others sound unpleasant (Crystal, 2014). For instance, French has a longstanding reputation as the language of love. Its associations with romance, fashion, fine dining, and literature have helped cement its image as elegant and sophisticated. Its rhythm, nasal vowels, and soft consonants contribute to the impression of musicality. There’s even a popular notion that everything sounds better in French, including insults. In The Matrix Reloaded, the Merovingian declares, “I have sampled every language. French is my favorite—a fantastic language, especially to curse with.” He then launches into a string of obscenities. It’s an unconventional endorsement, but it captures the seductive reputation that French has acquired.

The German language often gets a less flattering reception. It’s regularly described as harsh, guttural, or aggressive. The Irish comedian Dylan Moran once joked that German “sounds like a typewriter eating tinfoil being kicked down the stairs.” Its consonant clusters and sharp sounds might contribute to this impression, but our reactions are also affected by cultural stereotypes. German speakers are sometimes portrayed as cold, rigid, and overly concerned with rules and order. Historical associations with World War II and Nazi Germany have also influenced negative perceptions of the language. These stereotypes have a long history. The 16th-century Holy Roman Emperor Charles V once said that he spoke Spanish to God, Italian to women, French to men, and German to his horse.

Of course, French isn’t inherently romantic, and German isn’t naturally angry. No accent is objectively more intelligent, attractive, or pleasant than any other. These impressions are learned, reinforced by cultural representations, historical associations, media portrayals, and even our own personal experiences with the accent.

What sounds sophisticated to one listener might sound pretentious to someone else. What sounds friendly and familiar to one person might sound provincial to another. These judgments can have serious real-world consequences. Accent prejudice can influence hiring decisions, education, healthcare and legal outcomes, social relationships, and how much credibility we give someone. We might like to think we’re judging people based on what they say, but sometimes we’re making up our minds before we’ve even heard their point of view.

Perhaps the next time we find ourselves admiring or disliking someone’s accent, it’s worth considering what we’re really responding to. Is it the sounds themselves, or the stories, stereotypes, and biases we’ve attached to them?Learn more in my new book, Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language.

Stollznow, K. 2026. Beyond Words: How We Learn, Use, and Lose Language. Cambridge University Press.

Barrett, R., Cramer, J., & McGowan, K. B. 2023. English With an Accent: Language, Ideology, and Discrimination in the United States. Routledge.

Crystal, D., & Crystal, B. 2014. You Say Potato: The Story of English Accents. Pan Macmillan.

#4815. Ultra-Processed Food Intake May Increase Dementia, Stroke Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Your hub for heart health management, insights, and solutions

Healthy adults who eat high levels of ultra-processed foods (UPFs) may be more likely to show signs of damage to the brain that could increase the likelihood of stroke and future memory problems, according to a study published October 15 in JAMA Network Open.

UPFs are often defined using the NOVA classification: These foods typically have 5 or more ingredients and include substances not typically found in culinary preparations. This category of foods includes packaged snack foods, sugary cereals, soft drinks, and frozen ready-to-eat meals.

UPFs account for more than 50% of daily energy intake in high-income countries, including the United States, Canada, and the United Kingdom.

Previous research has linked these foods to adverse cardiometabolic outcomes. This new study adds to growing evidence linking high UPF intake to adverse health outcomes.

This was a cross-sectional analysis of 8,783 adults between the ages of 35 and 69 without cardiovascular disease. The participants were all enrolled in the Canadian Alliance for Healthy Hearts and Minds (CAHHM) and Prospective Urban and Rural Epidemiology-MIND (PURE-MIND) cohorts.

The researchers used MRI scans to evaluate the participants’ brains. They also set out to analyze the cross-sectional relationship between UPF consumption, body fat, vascular brain injury (VBI), and cognitive performance.

They measured the participants’ habitual UPF intake using a food frequency questionnaire. Intake was expressed as servings based on a 2,000-calorie-per-day diet.

UPFs accounted for an average of 25% of participants’ daily diets. For the individuals with the highest intake, this increased to 45% of everything on their plates, compared to 16% for those who ate the least.

The researchers also noted that UPFs were not just an added part of individual diets. These foods appeared to replace whole foods.

Among people with the highest UPF intake, fruits, vegetables, grains, and other minimally processed foods accounted for 41% of their daily food intake. Among those with the lowest UPF intake, minimally processed foods made up 68% of their daily intake.

When the researchers compared the highest intake to the lowest, they found that those with a higher intake of UPFs had 1.7% more body fat. They also found that people with a higher UPF intake had higher odds of VBI.

“These findings are concerning, but it is important to remember that an association does not prove cause and effect,” said Michelle Routhenstein, Preventive Cardiology Dietitian at Entirely Nourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“From my perspective as a preventive cardiology dietitian, these findings reinforce the importance of nourishing our blood vessels to support both cardiovascular and brain health.”

Although researchers found no significant differences in cognitive performance, the signs of vascular brain injury observed in the study have been associated with an increased risk of stroke and cognitive decline.

These findings suggest a possible link between UPF intake and signs of brain changes. However, participants were only assessed once and weren’t followed over time. This means the researchers were unable to determine whether UPFs directly caused the changes.

“While we can’t conclude from this study that limiting UPFs would improve brain health, we have decades of literature demonstrating that higher intakes of green leafy vegetables, brightly colored fruits, whole grains, and lean protein sources are good for brain health,” said Suzanne Judd, PhD, Director of the UC College of Medicine’s Center for Public Health, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“So focusing more on what can be brought into the diet rather than what should be eliminated might be a good way to start,” she added.

The preservatives [in UPFs] may have a direct impact on the vascular system, while the loss of antioxidants results in a less robust response to inflammation in the body.

“Additionally, sugar or salt is often added to make the food a bit tastier so people consume it in higher quantities. Over-consumption of food can lead to weight gain and diabetes, which can negatively impact brain health,” Judd said.

Judd told Healthline that it is virtually impossible to completely avoid UPFs. Even some “health” foods, like protein powder and some yogurts, are considered ultra-processed.

It is more important to look at diet overall and emphasize consuming foods as close to their natural state as possible, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and meats purchased raw or frozen and then cooked at home.

Routhenstein recommended starting simply with one manageable swap rather than trying to overhaul your entire diet.

She said that you should identify an ultra-processed food you eat regularly and consider a more nutrient-rich alternative. It is important to account for convenience, food preferences, budget, and lifestyle so that the change feels realistic and is sustainable over the long term.

“I want people to feel empowered, not fearful, when making food choices,” said Routhenstein. “Healthy eating does not mean having to cook everything from scratch. What matters most is building consistent, nourishing habits that support both heart and brain health.”

#4814. Honda has dominated motorcycles for decades. Electric bikes are changing that

Honda has spent decades building one of the most dominant positions in the global motorcycle industry, selling millions of gasoline-powered two-wheelers each year. But in markets where electric motorcycles and scooters are becoming increasingly accessible, that dominance is starting to face a serious challenge.

Vietnam offers a particularly interesting case study, where rapidly growing electric motorcycle sales are beginning to reshape a market long dominated by Honda.

According to newly released nationwide sales figures, Vietnam saw more than 3 million motorcycle and scooter sales during the first nine months of 2026, representing 25.9% growth over the same period last year.

But the real story is in the electric segment, where sales surged 90.5% to reach 973,247 units. That means electric two-wheelers now account for approximately 32% of all new motorcycle and scooter sales in the country.

And the biggest beneficiary isn’t Honda. It’s actually Vietnamese electric vehicle manufacturer VinFast.

While Honda remains Vietnam’s largest motorcycle manufacturer overall, with sales growing 8.4% this year, VinFast has surged into second place with a staggering 152.1% increase in sales. Yamaha now sits in third place, followed by electric two-wheeler manufacturer Yadea in fourth.

Of the top four players, half are electric, and it’s precisely that half that is experiencing meteoric sales growth.

It’s an impressive reshuffling of a market that has traditionally been dominated by Japanese gasoline motorcycle manufacturers.

Vietnam’s transition hasn’t happened in a vacuum, either. Government efforts to reduce urban air pollution, including plans to restrict gasoline-powered motorcycles in parts of Hanoi, have helped create an increasingly favorable environment for electric alternatives.

Too bad for Honda but I'm thrilled to read about increasing sales of electric motorcycles. I don't live in or near Vietnam but the pollution from small gasoline engines affects everyone where the wind blows it.

And with companies like VinFast offering an expanding range of electric scooters and motorcycles, riders now have more practical alternatives to gasoline-powered models than ever before.

To be clear, Honda isn’t exactly struggling. Its motorcycle sales are still growing, and the Japanese giant remains the undisputed market leader in Vietnam. But its overall share of the market is shrinking, and its relatively modest growth compared to the exploding electric segment suggests that the market’s center of gravity is beginning to shift.

Vietnam may be just a single example, but it’s an important one of what can happen when electric two-wheelers become viable mainstream alternatives to gasoline motorcycles.

Honda has spent decades perfecting the gasoline motorcycle. The question now is how quickly it can adapt to a market that is increasingly interested in something else.

#4813. I imported a $2,000 electric truck from China. Five years later, here’s the truth

Five years ago, I did something that seemed pretty ridiculous at the time. I bought a $2,000 electric mini-truck from China, had it shipped across the oceans to the US, and put it to work on my parents’ property in Florida.

The little white mini electric truck became something of an internet sensation, with my original unboxing and testing video quickly racking up over 10 million views, plus several million more from the follow-up videos.

It also attracted plenty of skeptics who were convinced that a $2,000 Chinese electric truck would fall apart within months, rust into oblivion, or otherwise prove to be a spectacular waste of money. “Good thing it has a bed,” was a common refrain. “So you can collect all the pieces that fall off along the way.”

I gave an update after the first year, showing that the truck was doing great. But to be fair, one year doesn’t tell us much.

Well now it’s been over five years, and I recently returned to Florida to see how the little truck has held up after five trips around the sun on my parents’ homestead. And I’ve got to say, the results are pretty surprising.

So here’s the truth about how the truck is doing five years later. Oh, and if you want to see it in action, you can check out my update video here. Trust me, you’ll want to.

First, it’s important to understand that this truck hasn’t spent five years sitting in a garage as some kind of novelty vehicle. It’s been a genuine workhorse on my parents’ 10-acre homestead.

Over the years, we’ve used it to haul everything from mulch and sand to lumber, tree branches, logs, yard waste, and everything in between.

Its hydraulic dump bed makes it particularly useful for moving bulk materials around the property, like hauling mulch and then dumping it in their raised planting beds.

My dad even uses it as a mobile irrigation truck during Florida’s dry season. I built him a solar-powered pump system that fills a water bladder in the truck’s bed with water from his pond, allowing him to drive around watering his trees and plants.

By now, it’s been involved in practically every major landscaping and construction project my parents have tackled.

We’ve also made some improvements over the years. Early on, my dad and I replaced the ridiculously stiff factory suspension springs with softer ones, making the ride considerably more comfortable. We added a custom tow hitch and swapped the original street tires for aggressive off-road tires that work much better on the property’s sandy and muddy terrain.

The suspension upgrade did reduce how much weight we can comfortably carry, though. Load more than around 500 pounds (220 kg) of sand or other bulk materials into the bed, and the rear end starts squatting enough that our homemade tow hitch threatens to touch grass.

But for most of the work we do, it’s been an excellent little utility vehicle.

And before anyone asks, no, this isn’t a street-legal truck. It was never really designed for American roads, and we use it almost exclusively on private property. Sure, it’s hit the pavement a few times since they live out in the boonies and its normal to see tractors and other non-street-legal vehicles on country roads, but it’s not the most ideal vehicle for long distance transport at 25 mph (40 km/h).

Here’s the part that surprised me most: Almost everything still works.

The electric windows still zip up and down with the speed of a guillotine. The electric door locks work. The headlights work. The backup camera works. Even the air conditioning still blows impressively cold air.

I actually checked that last one with a thermal camera during my latest visit, and the air coming out of the vents was around 55°F (12°C). Not bad for a five-year-old air conditioning system in a $2,000 truck!

The windshield wiper still operates, but its range of motion has decreased significantly. It now stops around the middle of the driver’s field of vision, which isn’t ideal when Florida’s famous afternoon thunderstorms roll through.

The rearview mirror has also developed an annoying habit of falling off. We’ve glued it back on multiple times, and it looks like another round of adhesive surgery is coming soon.

Inside, there’s some minor upholstery damage on the driver’s seat, including a few small tears and stressed seams in the cheap faux-leather material that you can see in the video.

The passenger seat, which sees much less use, still looks nearly new. In another few years, I might just swap the two seats to get another half decade or so out of them before we need some upholstery repair.

One decorative plastic panel around the driver’s door handle has popped off, though I still have the piece and could probably snap it back into place with a bit of effort. It’s just aesthetic though, so it’s been a low-priority repair.

And that’s pretty much the extent of the mechanical and electrical problems we’ve encountered.

There haven’t been any major drivetrain failures, the hydraulic dump bed still works, and the truck continues to start up and drive just as reliably as it did when it was new.

It still gets used for lots of bulk jobs, material hauling, and sometimes just random transportation around the property.

One of the biggest predictions from critics five years ago was that this cheap Chinese truck would quickly dissolve into a pile of rust.

To be fair, there is some rust. But nowhere near as much as you might expect.

Most of the corrosion is concentrated in areas where the paint has been scratched or chipped, especially around the tailgate and cargo bed.

The rustiest spot is definitely the top lip of the tailgate, where we usually have long objects hanging out of the bed, such as shovels, ladders, lumber, etc. The paint has worn through on that edge, and the rust has inevitably started in those few spots.

The truck is stored outdoors under a lean-to roof that I built between two shipping containers, but we have a skid-steer in front of it and so the rear of the truck sticks out and gets rained on several times a week (or several times a day during the summer).

We applied a paint-on bed liner during the truck’s first year, which helped protect the metal for quite a while.

After four years of hauling dirt, rocks, branches, and other abrasive materials though, that coating has started wearing through in a few places.

Every time I’m shoveling mulch out of the bed and I hear that scrape of metal on metal, I cringe just a bit before remembering that the truck cost me $2,000 and doesn’t owe me anything at this point.

Speaking of being parked outdoors with the rear hanging out for the world (and the UV) to see, there’s clearly an effect on the truck’s wear.

You can absolutely see the difference in the paint and plastic components. The front headlight lenses are still crystal clear, while the rear taillight lenses have become noticeably cloudy from UV exposure.

Despite that, the truck’s basic structure remains solid, and the rust is mostly cosmetic and limited to the high-impact areas that tend to get beaten up repeatedly, as you’d expect in any self-respecting work truck.

Considering that Florida combines high humidity, frequent rain, and intense sunshine, I’d call that a pretty impressive result for a vehicle that cost less than many electric bicycles.

Since the truck lives at my parents’ property, my dad has actually spent far more time using it than I have.

And when I asked him how he felt about the purchase after five years, he was surprisingly enthusiastic.

He described the truck as an incredibly functional piece of equipment that has become an essential part of maintaining the property.

In fact, he pointed out that the truck has been involved in virtually every significant project they’ve completed over the past five years.

It isn’t the only electric utility vehicle on the property anymore. My parents also have a Kandi electric UTV, which has taken over some of the smaller daily chores thanks to its better suspension and more convenient dump bed operation (the bed also lowers under power) which helps my dad lift the trash and recycling bins and drive them down the long private road to the street on pickup day.

But when it’s time to haul bulky loads, long branches, or large quantities of dirt and mulch, the Changli is still the vehicle of choice.

My dad also pointed out something that tends to get lost in discussions about cheap Chinese EVs: the operating costs have been almost nonexistent.

A full charge costs a little over a dollar in electricity, and the truck has required remarkably little maintenance over the years.

Even after five years, he says it still puts a smile on his face every time he drives it.

Yes, the truck cost me $2,000. Or technically, the price was $2,080.00, and that’s what I paid to the factory. At that point, it was mine.

Of course, it was still in China though, and so I had to pay an international freight company to have it sent on a cargo ship to the US (nearly $2,000 by itself, if I recall correctly).

Then I had to pay the US Treasury a bunch of tariffs to help make sure American automotive companies don’t have to compete with these types of vehicles.

And I also had to hire a customs broker to handle the import documentation for me, etc.

So there were several thousand dollars of additional fees on top of it, but I still think it was worth it based on the incredible amount of use it has given us over the years.

Of course, there’s an important caveat here for anyone considering getting a vehicle like this.

Remember, this is a very basic, low-speed electric utility vehicle without the safety equipment, crash protection, or regulatory approvals you’d expect from a modern full-size pickup truck.

It’s not something I’d recommend as a replacement for a road-going vehicle.

This is a work truck for us. It moves material, tows trailers and boats, carries the trash cans a quarter mile to the street each week, etc. In that way, as a private-property work truck, it’s been fantastic.

But even though I’m calling it simple, that doesn’t mean it wasn’t made pretty well. The truck has hauled countless loads, survived five years of rough Florida weather, and required very little maintenance. Even its cheap interior and basic electronics have held up better than I expected.

I also have to give some credit to the modifications we made early on, especially the suspension and tire upgrades, which turned a quirky little imported vehicle into something much more practical for off-road work.

The biggest unknown is how much longer it will last. Unfortunately, the truck doesn’t have a proper odometer, so I can’t even tell you how many miles we’ve accumulated over five years of driving around the property.

I also can’t tell you anything about battery degradation, since we don’t know how far it has driven (due to the lack of odometer), and the fact that even on 10 acres, you just can’t get that far from an outlet. We generally charge the 6 kWh battery every couple weeks just to keep it topped up, but range was never an issue and hasn’t become one, at least not for our use case. If you needed to drive this thing to the next town over each day, it could be another story.

Nothing like being forced to drive massive four-door trucks that weigh as much as four cars because your country is protecting monopolist manufacturers and only allows their land yachts for sale.

Basically, there’s no indication that the mini-truck is nearing the end of its useful life.

My dad thinks it could easily serve another five or even ten years, and after seeing how well it’s survived its first five, I’m inclined to agree that there’s plenty of life left in it.

When I first bought this thing, plenty of people told me it was a terrible idea. Five years later, with the truck still hauling dirt, carrying branches, and generally earning its keep, I’m feeling pretty good about that decision. It’s done a lot more in its five years than many “real” pickup trucks do in their entire lives.

Not bad for a funny little electric truck from China.

#4812. Sight Loss Does Not Make Someone an Incomplete Person

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

Nadine, a research participant in a study on blindness, said that using a white cane in public often made her the center of attention. She explained: “…it’s difficult because sometimes you don’t want everyone to look at you when you walk into a room. Sometimes you just want to sneak in and go … I just want to blend in” (Konrad, 2021).

The white cane attracts the attention of sighted people because it signifies blindness, which evokes their fear about their own vulnerability and their curiosity about people they may rarely encounter in daily life (Paterson, 2013; Garland-Thomson, 2006).

The irony is that this attention-grabbing symbol of blindness often obscures the individuality of those using it, thereby transforming unique cane users into faceless ciphers of disability. As one blind woman put it: “I'm invisible. …Even in a room full of 100 people, I feel like I'm not seen” (Szilva, 2025, p. 63). The person disappears behind the white cane because, in the eyes of others, their disability is the essence of who they are. In fact, others tend to assume that the blind person’s disability explains their personality, motives, and behaviors (Nario-Redmond, 2020).

In this post, I will explore how the use of culturally acquired assumptions to interpret and evaluate the behaviors of visually impaired adults complicates how they view themselves and how they respond to sight loss.

The onset of sight loss most often occurs in middle age or after (Brinks et al., 2019; NHS England, 2024). The radical changes brought about by sight loss usually trigger an extended period of depression and anxiety, as people gradually make the journey from sightedness to blindness (Nyman et al., 2012). To forestall fully arriving at that destination, they may try to pass as sighted for as long as possible (Thurston, 2024).

Eventually, most people experiencing sight loss face reality, and some take advantage of services that teach the nonvisual skills needed to function effectively in their daily lives, despite limited availability (Kaldenberg et al., 2023). Learning to navigate the world with a white cane is perhaps the nonvisual skill most closely linked to feelings of shame, inferiority, and loss of identity (Berndtsson, 2025). When Alice began to use a cane, she described herself as almost subhuman:

When you have a disability, you’re not a whole person.…[That’s] what gives you this nagging feeling that somehow you don’t have the same human dignity, you’ve become a little less, a little lower, a little… well, you’re not a whole, complete person. (Berndtsson, 2025).

What might Alice have meant when she stated that she is not “a whole, complete person”? She likely was referring to what her culture has taught her about blindness and blind people. In childhood, we are exposed to and begin to learn stereotypic beliefs about a variety of social groups, including racial, gender, and disability groups (Devine, 1989; Farago et al., 2019).

People experiencing sight loss and other disabling impairments often view themselves and are viewed by others through the lens of cultural stereotypes that mark them as inferior and defective (Nario-Redmond, 2010, 2020; Ricker, 2023). The white cane is a powerful symbol of blindness that reminds its users of these stereotypic beliefs. The stereotypes characterize people with severe visual impairments as dependent, incompetent, and helpless.

A person is said to have “internalized stigma” when they have learned the stereotypes and use them to evaluate themselves (see Goffman, 1963). These stereotypic beliefs emphasize dependency, which suggests what might be meant by not being “a whole, complete person.” The majority of cultures in Western societies promote an ideal that may be called the “individualistic self” (Cushman, 1995; Markus & Kitayama, 1991).

This ideal views the self as an internal center of agency: the maker and implementer of decisions that require no help from others. The individualistic self consists of a unique combination of elements that underlie our actions: traits, abilities, values, preferences, and desires.

The self is considered to be “bounded”: It is contained within the mind/body, and is presumed to be the primary determinant of our actions. The self, in essence, is assumed to stand alone in choosing goals and directing actions to achieve them. Thus, in this view, a whole, complete person exhibits total self-sufficiency, self-reliance, and autonomy.

Alice is not alone in thinking that reduced independence, understood as a reduced ability to perform tasks without help, somehow reduces one’s worth and dignity. A participant in another study lamented his lost independence: “I was independent all my life, I've done everything by myself … I now have to rely on other people to help in many, many ways” (cited in Enoch et al., 2025, p. 1121).

Some researchers and disability scholars argue for a shift towards encouraging interdependence rather than independence as a goal for adapting well to blindness and low vision.

Kenneth Jernigan, who served for years as the president of the National Federation of the Blind (NFB), gave a speech in 1993 in which he explained to some student critics why he used a sighted guide at the 1992 NFB convention. He stated that, when his mind was occupied with planning and completing tasks, depending on someone to guide him allowed him to concentrate on important matters.

Eva Feder Kittay, a philosopher of disability ethics, has questioned the ideal of the independent self. She has argued that no one is truly independent. Everyone, whether they are disabled or nondisabled, relies on “invisible” networks of supportive relationships that help them with daily tasks (Gesser & Fietz, 2021).

In his 1993 address, Jernigan provided an example that illustrated the importance of this publicly invisible support system in the lives of people who would seem to embody the cultural ideal of the independent, self-reliant person. Lamar Alexander, the Secretary of Education, spoke at the previous year’s convention. Alexander had an assistant arrive a day ahead of time to take care of arrangements. He picked Alexander up at the airport, accompanied him to the meeting room, walked with him to the stage, met him after the talk, and drove him to the airport. Alexander was fully capable of doing all those things without help, but he just did not have the time. Jernigan mused: “If the Secretary had been blind, I wonder if somebody would have said, ‘Just look! He's not independent. He has to have a sighted person with him at all times.’”

For Kittay, needing assistance does not make us incomplete humans or unworthy of human dignity. Needing assistance and giving assistance to others is what being human is all about: They are central features of the human condition.

Furthermore, it is unclear, to say the least, how one can classify requests for help as:

Ultimately, the argument for this double standard seems to be an invalid one:

The stereotypes causing all the trouble hold a firm grasp on our thinking about disability. They have a powerful influence on how we view others and also on how we view ourselves. Their stubborn refusal to yield to reason helps to explain why adapting to disabling impairments such as blindness can be a lifelong process.

#4810. What Is Creatine HCl—and Is It Better Than Creatine Monohydrate?

CREATINE MONOHYDRATE HAS been seen as the gold standard in creatine use for years, so what’s up with creatine-HCl? This is a product that’s been showing up more on social media and supplement shelves.

People online have claimed that creatine-HCl helps you get swole quicker with greater performance benefits than the more commonly used creatine monohydrate. Considering that creatine-HCl products tend to cost more than creatine monohydrate, is it worth forking over the extra dough? Let’s investigate.

CREATINE-HCL STANDS FOR creatine hydrochloride. This is a salt form of creatine, explains Scott Keatley, RD, co-owner of Keatley Medical Nutrition Therapy. The main difference between hydrochloride and monohydrate is that creatine-HCl dissolves faster in water.

SOME PEOPLE ON TikTok claim that creatine-HCl is better because it’s absorbed more easily in the muscles and has no loading phase. While creatine-HCl dissolves more easily in water, Keatley says that doesn't automatically mean it leads to better results. The no-loading-phase claim is true, says Keatley, but monohydrate doesn’t require loading either.

“It's like the difference between a 99 percent and 100 percent,” says Albert Matheny, RD, CSCS, co-founder of SoHo Strength Lab. “There's not a meaningful difference to you as a consumer.” Matheny argues that creatine-HCl's rise in popularity really comes from good, strategic marketing.

Shane Davis, MD, sports medicine physician and physiatrist at Tufts Medical Center, has dug into any scientific evidence that could justify creatine-HCl as a better alternative for building muscle. But he says there’s really nothing out there that points to creatine-HCl as a superior option to creatine monohydrate.

One study split 40 participants into groups to compare the effects of each form of creatine. After eight weeks, the researchers found that both forms “significantly enhanced” the effects of resistance training but showed “no benefit” of using creatine-HCl over creatine monohydrate.

THE CLEAREST ADVANTAGE Keatley sees is that creatine-HCl is easier to mix into a drink than creatine monohydrate since it dissolves more readily. Because of that, proponents for creatine-HCl also market the supplement as more gut-friendly and usable in smaller doses.

While some people find that creatine-HCl is easier on the stomach, there isn't strong evidence that it consistently causes fewer digestive issues, Keatley says. “Claims that much smaller doses deliver the same benefits also haven’t been convincingly established,” he continues. “I’d describe better solubility as a real advantage, while the other claims run ahead of the evidence.”

Ultimately, when asked if creatine-HCl is worth the extra splurge, dietitians were unanimous in saying it’s just pure marketing fluff; it’s all creatine at the end of the day.

#4809. A Handful of Pistachios May Help You Sleep Better, Review Says

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Could a handful of pistachios before you go to bed really help you sleep better?

A review of studies published in Nutrition Research Reviews examines how the nutrients and plant compounds in pistachios might influence sleep health.

Pistachios contain several nutrients linked to sleep-related processes, prompting an investigation into whether they might offer benefits beyond their nutritional value.

While the findings suggest that pistachios may support sleep, the evidence is inconclusive and warrants further study.

“Pistachios are compelling for sleep research because they bring together several nutrients and plant compounds connected to sleep physiology within one whole food,” said study author Marie-Pierre St-Onge, PhD, professor of nutritional medicine and director of the Center of Excellence for Sleep & Circadian Research in the Department of Medicine at Columbia University Institute of Nutrition, in a news release.

“Rather than focusing on a single ‘sleep nutrient,’ this review provides a rationale for studying how the complete pistachio food matrix may affect sleep-related pathways,” she continued.

The narrative review examined existing research on pistachios and sleep-related biology.

The researchers explored whether the combination of nutrients in pistachios could promote quality sleep.

Rather than identifying pistachios as a sleep remedy, the researchers outlined biological pathways through which their nutrients and bioactive compounds might influence sleep.

“We were particularly interested in pistachios because they are particularly high in phytomelatonin, polyphenols, and carotenoids, which we noted were plant-derived components that had been shown to have sleep benefits in preclinical studies,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“We also noted their high content of tryptophan and vitamin B6, which are relevant to melatonin production in humans,” she continued.

Pistachios contain several nutrients associated with sleep, including melatonin, which helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle.

Other studies examining the effects of some of these nutrients on sleep offer further context.

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of tryptophan supplementation found that it may reduce wakefulness after sleep onset, particularly at doses of at least 1 gram (g) daily. However, an ounce of pistachios supplies only about 71 mg, which is much less than the doses examined by the researchers.

Additionally, a 2023 review of dietary polyphenols led by St-Onge identified potential links between plant compounds and sleep outcomes, although results varied across studies.

Neither review established that polyphenols or tryptophan from pistachios specifically affected sleep quality.

“I was not surprised that pistachios may help support sleep, given their combination of nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” said Michelle Routhenstein, MS, a preventive cardiology dietitian at EntirelyNourished, who wasn’t involved in the study.

“Pistachios provide tryptophan, an amino acid the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin; vitamin B6, which supports these pathways; and magnesium, which plays a role in nervous system function and sleep regulation,” she told Healthline.

The new review highlights the concept of the “food matrix,” or how nutrients and bioactive compounds interact within a whole food.

Instead of investigating tryptophan, magnesium, or melatonin individually, researchers were curious about the combined effects of consuming them together in pistachios.

Laboratory and simulated-digestion research offers clues about how fiber and plant compounds in pistachios and peanuts interact with gut microbes. However, these findings do not establish that eating pistachios changes sleep quality in real-world conditions.

Broader nutrition research also points to a relationship between diet and sleep.

A 2021 review in the Annual Review of Nutrition examined evidence linking dietary patterns and individual nutrients to sleep outcomes. The findings suggest a relationship between sleep and diet, but note that more research is needed to determine cause and effect.

In a nutshell, the current evidence builds a compelling case for pistachios as a sleep aid.

However, it’s too soon to recommend pistachios as a sleep remedy, as many factors may affect sleep quality and insomnia.

“Sleep difficulties can have different underlying causes,” Routhenstein noted. “If inadequate intake of these nutrients is a contributing factor, pistachios may help, but they may not address sleep issues related to other nutrient deficiencies or other causes.”

Much of the supporting evidence cited in the review comes from studies of individual nutrients, other foods, laboratory experiments, or biological mechanisms rather than from trials involving whole pistachios.

Researchers have also reported significant variations in the melatonin content of pistachios, making the amount in a typical serving difficult to pinpoint.

Additionally, the review received support from American Pistachio Growers, and the corresponding author, St-Onge, serves on its advisory board. Larger studies and clinical trials are needed, ideally without industry funding, to ensure well-rounded results.

Indeed, the authors call for randomized controlled trials examining whether eating pistachios affects sleep outcomes, including sleep quality, duration, and melatonin levels.

“This was a review; we noted that the complete profile of pistachios would make them well-suited to support healthful sleep, but research is needed to evaluate this,” St-Onge told Healthline.

“This is the next step, and something we are actively working on. We also need to better understand what dosage and frequency of consumption would be optimal.”

Regardless, a handful of pistachios is still considered a healthy choice as part of a balanced diet.

“A small handful, about 1 ounce of shelled pistachios, is an appropriate portion,” Routhenstein said. “Enjoy them during the day or as a light afternoon or evening snack when you’re hungry.”

If nutrients like tryptophan help promote sleep, it’s possible that other nuts could yield similar results.

“Other nuts, such as almonds and walnuts, may offer similar benefits because they also contain nutrients involved in sleep regulation,” Routhenstein said.

“Early research is encouraging, but it’s too soon to say how much they might help.”

Other foods, like turkey, also contain tryptophan.

“For someone allergic to nuts, foods such as tofu, beans, oats, eggs, dairy, and fish can provide tryptophan, which the body uses to make serotonin and melatonin,” Routhenstein said. “The goal is to meet their nutrient needs rather than rely on one food to improve sleep.”

Sleep health depends on multiple factors. As such, Routhenstein recommends a personalized approach to getting better sleep, from what you eat and when you eat to addressing any nutritional gaps.

“I would also encourage regular, balanced meals throughout the day to support blood sugar management, especially for those with diabetes, while avoiding large meals close to bedtime,” Routhenstein said. “Caffeine later in the day and alcohol in the evening are also worth considering as possible sleep disruptors.”

#4806. What If Nothing Is Wrong With You?

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Posted November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Ekua Hagan

In my nearly two decades as a therapist, I’ve sat with hundreds of people of all ages and backgrounds, and one thing has become clear: By adulthood, feeling inherently lovable and worthy seems to be the exception rather than the rule.

The quiet belief that “something is fundamentally wrong with me” is a burden so many of us carry as we move through life, often without even realizing it. Psychologist and Buddhist meditation teacher Tara Brach describes this as living under “the trance of unworthiness.” It may sound like:

But we don’t start out this way. “Babies don't wonder whether they deserve to be seen, connected with, or held,” says Jackie Ourman, LMHC, couples and individual therapist at Values Aligned Therapy and founder of Social Connection Collective. “Our earliest relationships teach us about our value through the ways the people who are supposed to care for us respond to our needs.”

What we learned, we can begin to unlearn.

Consider these practices to help you awaken from the trance of unworthiness.

1. Recognize you're in the trance of unworthiness.

When we are caught in the trance, deeply rooted negative beliefs can feel like indisputable facts. Ourman encourages her clients to notice that what they are experiencing is a thought, not necessarily a fact.

“There’s a difference,” Ourman says, “between saying, ‘I’m not enough’ and saying, ‘I’m having the thought that I’m not enough.’ This creates a little distance from our thoughts so we don’t automatically believe everything our minds tell us.”

Simply noticing that we are in the midst of a self-critical inner monologue is a powerful act in itself. That is mindfulness: observing thoughts without judgment and without being swept away by them.

In her book, Radical Acceptance, Brach describes a practice she calls the “sacred pause,” drawing on Buddhist teachings. The next time you notice yourself spiraling, stop and take a breath. Notice what’s happening in your body and which thoughts have arrived. Resist the urge to fix, explain, or dismiss what you feel. Then ask yourself:

“What does my heart truly long for in this moment?”

Not “what would make me more impressive or more acceptable to others.” Simply, “What does your heart truly long for right now?” Ask again, and wait.

The pause gives us an opportunity to listen more deeply and reconnect with our soul voice, the one within us that knows what we truly need.

3. Send compassion to the little you who took on the burden of “not good enough.”

For many of us, it's easier to offer compassion to our child selves than to our present selves. If this resonates, try this exercise.

Find the most endearing photo you can of yourself as a child. One that evokes warmth or tenderness. Spend some time looking into the little one’s eyes. See their desire to belong, or their simple wish to be loved. Then ask yourself:

What did that little one need to hear? What did they need to know about themselves? Perhaps they needed to know that their needs weren’t too much, or that they weren’t responsible for the things that happened to them.

4. See yourself through the eyes of those who love you.

When we’re caught in the trance of unworthiness, our view of ourselves can become remarkably narrow. We fixate on our perceived flaws and overlook the qualities others see so clearly.

Think of a person who genuinely loves you; someone who sees you with affection. What might they say about you? What qualities would they notice that you routinely overlook? What would they remind you of when you are convinced that you have nothing worthwhile to offer?

This is not about depending on others’ approval to feel okay. It is about recognizing that our self-perception isn’t always reliable and never fully captures who we are.

5. Understand where the beliefs came from.

When we begin to understand how our negative beliefs originated, we can extend compassion to the younger version of ourselves who was simply trying to make sense of their experiences.

“I think it's important to acknowledge and validate those early experiences while also recognizing that the conclusions someone drew about themselves may not be true,” says Ourman. “For many people, the work is less about building worth from scratch and more about finding their way back to it.”

You don’t have to believe you are worthy overnight. These old beliefs may have been with you for a long time, but with patience, they can begin to loosen. Start with one small practice, whichever one speaks to you.

May you be kind to yourself and find your way back to the worth that was always there.

Brach, Tara. (2003) Radical Acceptance: Embracing Your Life with the Heart of a Buddha. Bantam.

Brach, T. (2019). Radical compassion: Learning to love yourself and your world with the practice of RAIN. Viking/Penguin Random House.

Ourman, J. (2026, October). Email interview.

#4805. ACOG Strongly Recommends Hormone Therapy for Menopause Symptoms

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) published updated recommendations for menopause management in Obstetrics & Gynecology on October 15.

These expanded recommendations are the most comprehensive guidance to date. They include new clinical guidelines for menopause hormone therapy (MHT), nonhormonal medications, and nonpharmacological treatment of vasomotor symptoms (VMS), which include hot flashes and night sweats, and sleep and mood changes.

According to the ACOG guidance, 50%–92% of females experiencing menopause report VMS.

Around 16%–66% of females in the United States report menopause-related sleep issues, and more than one-third of perimenopausal and postmenopausal females report experiencing depressive symptoms.

“In recent years, misconceptions about the risks of hormone therapy have been widespread, which has made some clinicians reluctant to prescribe it and some patients hesitant to use it,” Bruce Pier, MD, clinical professor and associate fellowship director at the University of North Carolina and collaborator on the ACOG clinical practice guidelines, told Healthline.

“This guidance offers a comprehensive review of the evidence to support individualized counseling and shared decision making. Our hope is that it clears up those misconceptions and expands access to treatment.”

The ACOG is also developing companion guidance for genitourinary syndrome of menopause, expected in 2027.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of MHT with estrogen and progestogens (or estrogen alone for people without a uterus) for both VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbance, in individuals who can use hormones.

It also conditionally recommends conjugated estrogen plus bazedoxifene (Duavee) as an alternative for these issues.

According to a meta-analysis from 2021 that was cited by the guidelines, estrogen therapy, with or without progestogens, significantly reduced VMS frequency and severity compared to a placebo or no treatment. A 2017 meta-analysis ranked transdermal estradiol plus a progestogen as the most effective option for reducing VMS frequency.

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis, also cited by the guidelines, found that MHT was associated with improved self-reported sleep quality. Once again, transdermal therapies showed some of the largest effects.

The ACOG recommends initiating MHT before age 60 or within 10 years of the onset of natural menopause..

It also suggests that the decision to start MHT for VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances should be based on a shared decision making discussion about an individual’s symptoms and the benefits and risks of therapy. Consideration should also be taken regarding an individual’s:

Research shows that factors such as race, culture, socioeconomic status, gender identity, and sexual orientation can influence how individuals experience menopause and the care they receive.

According to the SWAN study, Black women reported more menopause symptoms than white women but were less likely to be treated for them.

“This updated document shines a light on these inequities. Clinicians can proactively help right now by asking every patient in midlife about symptoms, rather than waiting for them to bring it up. Long term, we hope this document drives more research funding to understand these gaps and begin closing them,” said Pier.

The ACOG stated in the guidelines that, “The available evidence is insufficient to recommend for or against the use of estrogen–progestogen or estrogen-only MHT for the treatment of menopause-related depressive symptoms.”

It recommends that perimenopausal and postmenopausal individuals who meet the diagnostic criteria for major depressive disorder (MDD) or those whose most noticeable symptom is depression should be treated according to depression management guidelines.

Current treatment guidelines for depression include therapy, medication, or a combination of the two.

Psychological treatments for depression include psychotherapy, such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), while antidepressants are among the most commonly prescribed medications.

The ACOG strongly recommends the use of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) for the management of menopausal symptoms like VMS and depression in individuals who don’t want to use MHT or can’t use it.

Currently, paroxetine is the only antidepressant that is approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the management of VMS.

The ACOG also strongly recommends the use of neurokinin receptor antagonists to manage VMS and vasomotor-related sleep disturbances in people who don’t desire hormone therapy or can’t use it.

There are currently two neurokinin receptor antagonists approved by the FDA to manage menopause symptoms. Fezolinetant (Veozah) was approved in 2023 to help manage hot flashes. In 2025, the FDA approved elinzanetant (LYNKUET) for the management of moderate to severe VMS due to menopause.

Another nonhormonal treatment for VMS that the ACOG conditionally recommends is gabapentin.

There are various nonpharmacologic treatments that the ACOG conditionally recommends for the management of VMS, vasomotor-related sleep disturbances, and mood changes. These are treatments that don’t involve the use of medications.

The nonpharmacologic treatments conditionally recommended include:

It is generally recommended that these interventions are used alongside hormonal or nonhormonal medications.

The ACOG noted that there is not enough evidence to support the efficacy or safety of phytoestrogens, such as soy isoflavones, or herbal supplements, which are not regulated by the FDA in the same way medications are for safety, purity, or efficacy.

“Menopause is finally getting the attention it deserves, and this document shows what evidence-based care should look like in this space. It lays out a range of safe, effective options for managing menopause symptoms. My message to anyone struggling with these symptoms is simple: talk to your clinician. You don’t have to suffer through them,” said Pier.

#4802. Why We Can’t Go It Alone

After years or decades, problems and patterns can become deeply entrenched. Be a fly on the wall during a sample couples therapy session and witness the slow, deliberate work of changing those patterns for a more enduring love.

Self Tests are all about you. Are you outgoing or introverted? Are you a narcissist? Does perfectionism hold you back? Find out the answers to these questions and more with Psychology Today.

Updated November 9, 2026 | Reviewed by Monica Vilhauer Ph.D.

If a formula for achieving happiness existed, most of us would be following it to the letter. It would also be a global money-making business, marketed in every country. You could buy it online, and perhaps it would even be taught in schools and universities. But happiness doesn’t have a blueprint. It can’t be ordered with free two-day shipping.

So, what is the origin of happiness? Perhaps it comes from finding meaning and purpose in our short existence? Or pursuing a fulfilling career? Embracing spirituality? Is it a result of having love in our lives? Or some other source?

These days, it seems that most happiness-boosting approaches point towards building up your individuality and focusing on you. For decades, we have all been marinating in the self-help ethos that prescribes the inward shift to the self as the only way to foster happiness. Social media, especially, drives that pop psychology viewpoint.

But experts tell us that the biggest influence on happiness (not necessarily the exact cause of it) is being around people and getting along with them. It’s also in the value of our family ties, our intimate partnerships, and our friendships. Therefore, if you are planning to outlive everyone that you know, your social circle needs to consist of more than just your houseplants and a cat. You may need to mix it up a little and find a few human souls.

The 2023 book, The Good Life: Lessons from the World's Longest Scientific Study of Happiness, underlines how significantly our well-being is linked to our human relationships. For example, one of the many studies found that “the people who were the most satisfied in their relationships at age 50 were the healthiest (mentally and physically) at age 80." In other words, healthy relationships and strong bonds help us not only to prosper, but live longer too.

Our ability to adapt to fellow humans and learn how to deal with all the ups and downs that relationships cause is key to contentment. When we engage with other people as our imperfect selves, and we feel safe and accepted, it refutes the illusion that happiness lies only within the self. This speaks to what so many of us consider one of life's decisive objectives: finding someone who embraces us for who we genuinely are. If we are lucky enough to find that, it makes life feel pretty good.

Also, we all know the exceptional joy of connecting with like-minded souls—those who mirror our experiences and share our passions. Sharing moments and activities with others not only reduces loneliness and breeds a sense of universality, but it also makes us feel secure. Having people who can bear witness to our milestones, achievements, and even our sorrows is invaluable.

So even if you like being alone, as humans, we are and have always been social creatures that need each other for survival. We didn’t evolve for thousands of years in a vacuum. Plus, research also shows that in the long run, engaging with others and hopefully finding people to love gives our lives the most significance. It also gives us our identity by reflecting back to us our own humanity.

Psychoanalyst Stephen A. Mitchell, from his book Relational Concepts in Psychoanalysis: Integration, said, “We live in a relational matrix. The person is comprehensible only within this tapestry of relationships, past or present.” In other words, the quality of our relationships clarifies us. Without them, we are inadequate, searching in the dark for a likeness we can only find in our fellow humans. Perhaps when we find the likeness, we find the joy.

Hence, stop looking for the undisclosed blueprint and discover why the ultimate happy formula may not be a solo project—it might be the people right next to you.

But for those of you who are less inclined to place a premium on close and familial connections, here are a few other important factors to happiness that cannot be denied or ignored. Acknowledging and practicing these sustainable aspects of living could additionally help make you more content on a regular basis.

For example, having gratitude for what you have. Secondly, connecting to your own interpretation of God or a higher power. And thirdly, having a sense of purpose and goals.

Look at happiness as a series of actions to exercise every day, not a destination to reach or something you can add to your shopping cart. Remember, humans are not built for separateness; you will be better off sharing some parts of your life with others. Therefore, don’t look at it as an “all or nothing” thing. Find the nuance, the gray area where you can connect and spend time with others without compromising your “alone” time. Isolation is the new smoking.

Mitchell, S. A. (1988). Relational concepts in psychoanalysis: An integration. Harvard University Press.

Yalom, I. D., & Leszcz, M. (2020). The theory and practice of group psychotherapy (6th ed.). Basic Books.

Lieberman, M. D. (2013). Social: Why our brains are wired to connect. Crown.
